messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 57
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: North American
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tutor
- Trauma Type: Sexual assault
- Pcl5: 66

**Case Vignette: “Mr. A.”**

Mr. A. is a 57-year-old, single North American man who has been attending sessions for the past three weeks. He presents as a soft-spoken, meticulously dressed man who sits with his hands folded in his lap, his posture rigid. He is a private tutor, specializing in advanced mathematics and physics for high school and college students. He describes his work as “the only place where the rules are clear.”

He begins his story slowly. For thirty years, he worked as a senior engineer at a large tech firm. He was respected, quiet, and kept to himself. He had a small circle of friends but never married. He attributes this to being “too much in my own head.” Five years ago, he was assaulted by a colleague during a late-night project deadline. The colleague, a man he had trusted and worked beside for over a decade, cornered him in a storage room. Mr. A. describes the event with clinical detachment: “It was a violation of professional trust. That’s the framework I use.” He did not report the assault. He told no one. He quit his job the following week, citing burnout.

After leaving the firm, Mr. A. began tutoring. He works from a small home office, his desk facing the door, his back to the wall. He says he chose this profession because it allows him to control his environment. “I set the schedule. I choose the students. I know exactly what will happen in each session.” He tutors three to four students a day, but he has begun to dread the sessions. He finds himself scanning the faces of his students—teenagers and young adults—for signs of betrayal. He once had to stop a session with a 19-year-old male student because the student leaned forward to look at a diagram, and Mr. A. felt a sudden, suffocating pressure in his chest. He excused himself to the bathroom and stood with his hands on the sink, breathing in short, sharp gasps. He has not scheduled that student again.

At night, Mr. A. sleeps in a recliner in his living room. He cannot sleep in his bed. He says the bedroom feels “exposed.” He keeps the television on low, tuned to a nature documentary channel. He finds the narrator’s voice calming. He wakes multiple times each night, drenched in sweat, his heart pounding. He does not remember specific nightmares, only a feeling of being trapped, of a heavy weight on his chest. He has not had a full night’s sleep in over four years.

He has developed a series of elaborate rituals. Before every tutoring session, he checks the locks on his front door three times. He arranges his pens and calculators in a precise order. He will not answer the door if he does not know the person. He has stopped going to the grocery store after 6 p.m. because the aisles feel “too narrow.” He describes a constant, low-level hypervigilance. “I am always aware of where the exits are. In a restaurant, I sit facing the door. In a waiting room, I choose a seat that allows me to see everyone.” He says this matter-of-factly, as if describing a survival strategy.

Mr. A. has not had a romantic relationship in over a decade. He says he “doesn’t trust anyone that way anymore.” He has no close friends. His only regular social contact is with his students. He feels a deep shame about the assault, a shame he cannot articulate. “I should have been stronger. I should have seen it coming. I am a logical person. I should have seen the signs.” He blames himself for being “too naive.”

He has begun to isolate further. He has canceled three tutoring sessions in the past two weeks, claiming illness. He spends his days in his apartment, watching documentaries, checking his locks, and waiting for the next session to begin. He describes a feeling of being “on a very long, very quiet train. I am watching the world go by through a window I cannot open.” He has no plans for the future. He lives in a suspended present, a present that feels like a waiting room.
